'''''Corymbia ficifolia''''', commonly known as '''red flowering gum''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Corymbia ficifolia'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/corymbia_ficifolia.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=6 June 2020}}</ref> is a species of small tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to the [[South West (Western Australia)|south-west]] of Western Australia. It has rough, fibrous bark on the trunk and branches, egg-shaped to broadly lance-shape adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven, bright red, pink or orange flowers and urn-shaped fruit. It has a restricted distribution in the wild but is one of the most commonly planted ornamental eucalypts.

==Description==
''Corymbia ficifolia'' is a straggly tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|10|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has rough, fibrous brownish bark on the trunk and branches. The adult leaves are dull to slightly glossy, paler on the lower surface, egg-shaped to broadly lance-shaped, {{cvt|70-130|mm}} long and {{cvt|25-50|mm|1}} wide, tapering to a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|8-20|mm|1}} long. The flower buds are arranged on the ends of branchlets on a branched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|15-32|mm|1}} long, each branch of the peduncle with seven buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|13-27|mm|1}} long. Mature buds are oval to pear-shaped, {{cvt|12-18|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|6-8|mm}} wide with a rounded to flattened [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs from December to May and the flowers are bright red to pink to orange. The fruit is a woody urn-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|20-42|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|18-30|mm|1}} wide with the valves enclosed in the fruit.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name=dn>{{cite web|url=http://www.australiangeographic.com.au/topics/science-environment/2010/04/guide-to-australias-gum-blossoms/|title=An illustrated guide to Australia's gum blossoms|author=Dean Nicolle|author-link=Dean Nicolle|publisher=Australian Geographic|date=30 April 2010|access-date=19 November 2017}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus ficifolia'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Corymbia%20ficifolia |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment, Canberra |access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref><ref name="Telopea">{{cite journal |last1=Hill |first1=Kenneth D. |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=Systematic studies in the eucalypts. 7. A revision of the bloodwoods, genus ''Corymbia'' (Myrtaceae) |journal=Telopea |date=13 December 1995 |volume=6 |issue=2–3 |pages=245–247 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/57836810#page/77/mode/1up |doi=10.7751/telopea19953017|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The other two bloodwoods found in the south-west of Western Australia are ''[[Corymbia haematoxylon|C. haemotoxylon]]'' and marri (''[[Corymbia calophylla|C. calophylla]]''). Unlike ''C. ficifolia'', they have tessellated bark rather than fibrous bark.<ref name="CANBR" />

==Taxonomy==
Red-flowering gum was first formally described in 1860 by [[Ferdinand von Mueller]], who gave it the name ''Eucalyptus ficifolia'' and published the description in his book, ''[[Fragmenta Phytographiae Australiae]]''.<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus ficifolia''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455244|publisher=APNI|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref><ref name="F.Muell.">{{cite book |last1=von Mueller |first1=Ferdinand |title=Fragmenta phytographiae Australiae |date=1860 |volume=2 |publisher=Victorian Government Printer |location=Melbourne |page=85 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/7219#page/88/mode/1up |access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref> In 1995, [[Ken Hill (botanist)|Ken Hill]] and [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson]] changed the name to ''Corymbia ficifolia''.<ref name="Telopea" /><ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Corymbia ficifolia''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/562499|publisher=APNI|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

In 2009,  Parra-O and colleagues published a  combined analysis of nuclear rDNA (ETS + ITS) and morphological characters published to clarify relationships within the genus ''Corymbia''. ''C. ficifolia'' was shown to comprise a natural group with two other Western Australian species ''[[Corymbia calophylla|C. calophylla]]'' and ''[[Corymbia haematoxylon|C. haematoxylon]]''. They classified the group as section ''Calophyllae'' within the subgenus ''Corymbia''.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Parra-O. | first1 = C.| last2 = Bayly | first2 = M. J. | last3 = Drinnan | first3 = A. | last4 = Udovicic | first4 = F. | last5 = Ladiges | first5 = P. | title = Phylogeny, major clades and infrageneric classification of ''Corymbia''(Myrtaceae), based on nuclear ribosomal DNA and morphology | doi = 10.1071/SB09028 | journal = Australian Systematic Botany | volume = 22 | issue = 5 | pages = 384–399 | year = 2009 }}</ref>

The [[specific epithet]] ''ficifolia'' is from Latin ''ficus'' meaning 'fig' and ''folium'' 'leaf', referring to the similarity of its leaves to some species of ''[[Ficus]]''.<ref name="F.Muell." /><ref name="bgpa">{{cite web |title=''Corymbia ficifolia'' |url=https://www.bgpa.wa.gov.au/about-us/information/our-plants/plants-in-focus/corymbia-ficifolia |publisher=Government of Western Australia: Botanic Gardens and Park Authority |access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

The [[type specimen]] was collected from around the [[Broke Inlet]] by [[George Maxwell]].<ref name="CANBR" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Corymbia ficifolia'' grows in sandy soil in low forest on slopes and is restricted to a sub-coastal distribution south-east of [[Perth]], east of [[Mount Frankland National Park|Mount Frankland]], [[Walpole, Western Australia|Walpole]] and the [[Stirling Range]].<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase | name = ''Corymbia ficifolia''| id = 17103}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
Red-flowering gum is one of the most widely cultivated of all eucalypts, both in Australia and overseas. It is best suited to temperate districts with low summer rainfall and is rarely reliable on the east coast of Australia. In suitable climates it is moderately fast-growing and is often larger and more vigorous in cultivation than in the wild. Eucalypts are difficult to grow from cuttings and are usually grown from seed. As a result, flower colour cannot be guaranteed, although some small forms have become available as grafted plants.<ref name="ANPSA">{{cite web |title=''Corymbia ficifolia'' |url=http://anpsa.org.au/c-fic.html |publisher=Australian Native Plant Society (Australia) |access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

In nature ''Corymbia ficifolia'' prefers infertile, sandy soils but it is readily adaptable to most temperate locations, provided it is not exposed to severe frost or sustained tropical damp. It is an ideal street tree as it is hardy, moderately fast growing, and rarely grows large enough to require pruning. The largest known single-stemmed tree of this species in the world (216.5 cm diameter) is located on Princes Street in Hamilton, New Zealand.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://register.notabletrees.org.nz/tree/view/32 | work = The Zealand Tree Register | title = Tree Information | access-date = 14 July 2011}}</ref> Because of its big and lovely colourful flowers, genetic improvement for cold resistance in [[Dublin]] area in [[Ireland]] is being carried out by collecting seeds in the coldest parts of Western and Southern Australia where it grows. In Ireland most of the plants were killed by severe frosts but the surviving [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s have been kept by [[tissue culture]].<ref name="The Garden Flora of Northern Ireland" >{{cite web|url=http://www.earlscliffe.com/climatic_zone_plants.htm|title=Climatic zone plants|publisher=Earlscliffe|access-date=2011-08-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721193555/http://www.earlscliffe.com/climatic_zone_plants.htm|archive-date=2011-07-21|url-status=dead}}</ref>
